subject: environmental-science
title: Mapping the Living Tapestry
welcome_lead: Step into the canopy where genes, species and ecosystems weave a single fabric of life.
meta_desc: A-Level Environmental Science adventure on biodiversity levels, indices and global hotspots.
final_note: Biodiversity is measured at three nested scales — protect one, you protect them all.

walkthroughs.body_html: Biodiversity has three nested scales: genetic sustains adaptation, species describes communities, ecosystem captures habitat variety.
Simpson's D emphasises dominance; Shannon's H' rewards evenness with values 1.5–3.5 in temperate forests.
Hotspots cover 2.4% of Earth but host 50% of endemic plants — e.g. Atlantic Forest, Sundaland, Mediterranean Basin.

mcqs.q: Which condition defines a biodiversity hotspot?
options: ≥1500 endemic plant species and ≥70% primary vegetation loss
≥500 endemic mammals only
Any tropical rainforest >1000 km²
Any tropical marine protected area

mcqs.q: Which index is most sensitive to dominant species?
options: Simpson's D
Shannon's H'
Margalef's index
Pielou's evenness

mcqs.q: What is the difference between species richness and species evenness?
options: It removes carbon permanently.
Richness counts how many species exist; evenness measures how balanced their abundances are.
They are the same measurement.
Richness is for plants, evenness for animals.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between in-situ and ex-situ conservation?
options: One is for plants, the other for animals.
Richness is for plants, evenness for animals.
In-situ protects species in their natural habitat; ex-situ removes them to controlled settings like zoos or seed banks.
They are alternative names for the same approach.

mcqs.q: Why is burning fossil fuels considered to disrupt the carbon cycle?
options: Richness is for plants, evenness for animals.
It releases carbon stored for millions of years much faster than the cycle can absorb.
It removes carbon permanently.
It creates new carbon that did not exist before.
